step1_summary.chief_complaint: New shortness of breath / chest tightness with wheeze for 2–3 days
symptoms: Dyspnoea now with brisk walking as well
Wheezing and dry cough, no sputum
Salbutamol (blue inhaler) gives minimal relief; using it daily ± qAM/qPM
No hospital admissions, no prior oral steroids
No fever, chest pain, sputum or haemoptysis mentioned
past_medical_history: Asthma (well-controlled until current episode, last attack 3–4 yrs ago)
step1_summary.vital_signs_exam: No vitals or physical exam performed during tele-consultation

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute onset dyspnoea in young female; however no risk factors documented
I: Viral upper respiratory tract infection / viral bronchitis: recent onset cough, wheeze, and SOB could reflect viral airway inflammation triggering asthma
Community-acquired pneumonia (atypical/early): cough and SOB, though no sputum or fever yet
N: Endobronchial neoplasm (e.g., carcinoid) causing obstruction & wheeze – unlikely but fits chronic asthma-like picture
D: Anemia / iron-deficiency leading to exertional dyspnoea – no data on pallor or fatigue but common cause
I2: Poor inhaler technique or inadequate dosing (iatrogenic) leading to loss of asthma control
C: Congenital airway anomaly (e.g., bronchiectasis) – chronic cough/wheeze though not supported
A: Allergic asthma exacerbation from new environmental trigger or seasonal pollen
T: Chest wall / rib trauma with pain-limited ventilation – no trauma reported
E: Thyrotoxicosis causing dyspnoea on exertion – no other hyperthyroid signs

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Asthma exacerbation (loss of control / exercise-induced or allergen-triggered)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Known asthmatic with sudden increase in wheeze, cough and SOB, minimal response to reliever, using preventer inconsistently; classic for mild asthma flare

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection triggering asthma symptoms (viral bronchitis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Commonest precipitant of acute asthma; 2–3-day history, cough, no sputum or fever yet
Symptoms started while running, may reflect EIB or sub-optimal inhaler delivery leading to poor control
Acute unexplained dyspnoea; but young, no risk factors, wheeze more suggestive of airway disease
Cough and SOB could represent early infection, but absence of fever, sputum, systemic features lowers probability

step4_evidence.diagnosis: Asthma exacerbation (loss of control / exercise-induced or allergen-triggered)
supporting_evidence: Triggered by exercise; worse over 2–3 days
Salbutamol needed more frequently but less effective
No prior attack for years – suggests new trigger/exacerbation rather than alternative disease
opposing_evidence: No objective decrease in peak-flow documented (patient hasn’t measured)
No mention of nocturnal symptoms or chest tightness at rest

step4_evidence.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection triggering asthma symptoms (viral bronchitis)
supporting_evidence: Abrupt onset over a few days
Cough and wheeze common with viral URTI
opposing_evidence: No sore throat, nasal congestion, fever or systemic viral symptoms described

supporting_evidence: Symptoms began during running and occur with brisk walking
Possible sub-optimal preventer dosing (3 puffs BID) or poor technique
opposing_evidence: Now symptomatic even at rest/brisk walk, suggesting broader loss of control rather than isolated EIB
Young age (26), no risk factors (immobility, OCP, surgery, pregnancy) provided
Presence of wheeze points to airway pathology
No pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, haemoptysis or syncope documented
No fever, chills or productive cough
